# FDG5128

> DO prefer named tuples over unnamed tuples (including `System.Tuple<T1, ...>` and `System.ValueTuple<T1, ...>`).

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 5.9 Using Tuples in Member Signatures.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG5128
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application none, test none
- Language: [C# 7+] (before that: Before C# 7.0 there are no named tuples; use a descriptive type (FDG5127).)
- Status: draft

Message: Name the elements of the tuple type '{0}' in the signature of '{1}'

Library only: see FDG5127. FDG5128 reports, once per member, an externally visible method, constructor, delegate, operator, property, indexer, field or event whose signature uses an unnamed tuple: System.Tuple<...>, or a value tuple with an element that has no name, such as (int, int) or ValueTuple<int, int>, also as a type argument or an array element type. Overrides and interface implementations are not reported. Replacing System.Tuple with a named tuple changes the type, so the fix is breaking; only adding names to a value tuple is not. There is no code fix.

## From the book

The previous section shows why descriptive types are better than named tuples in public API, as well as why named tuples are better than unnamed tuples. However, occasionally a method is so specialized that it would never make sense to amend the returned data, a custom descriptive type would only ever be deconstructed into locals, and the method name really is sufficient for documentation. When all of these conditions are true for a method’s return type, then a named tuple might make more sense. For example, .NET Standard 2.1 added `System.Range`, which has a utility method to compute the total length and initial offset for a range:

```csharp
public partial struct Range {
   public (int Offset, int Length) GetOffsetAndLength(int length);
}
```
